**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference cluster

**Status and context**

Our four A100 nodes are running hot. Peak-hour utilization sits around 85 percent, queue times for batch jobs have crept from minutes to hours, and interactive users are starting to notice latency in the notebook environment. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase two additional nodes, at roughly $180k all-in with networking and support, or invest a quarter of engineering time in squeezing more out of what we already own. I've spent the last two weeks looking at the data, and I want to lay out how I think we should reason about this before we commit either way.

**What the numbers actually say**

The utilization figure is misleading on its own. Eighty-five percent sounds like we're nearly maxed out, but a breakdown by time of day tells a different story. Overnight and weekend utilization drops below 30 percent, and a meaningful share of our peak load comes from jobs that are not latency-sensitive at all — model evaluation runs, embedding backfills, fine-tuning experiments. These are jobs that could tolerate a delay of several hours without anyone noticing. Right now they compete with interactive work for the same capacity because our scheduler treats them identically. A modest investment in workload segregation, better preemption, and autoscaling our batch queue into the off-peak window would, by my estimate, free up 20 to 25 percent of peak capacity. That is the equivalent of roughly one additional node, purchased with engineer-weeks rather than capital.

There is also waste we can eliminate outright. Two teams are holding reservations on GPUs they use intermittently, and our current accounting makes it easier to squat on hardware than to release and re-request it. Fixing the incentive structure — showback rather than soft reservations, with a fast path for reclaiming idle capacity — costs almost nothing and recovers real headroom.

**The case for buying anyway**

That said, I don't want to oversell optimization. Some of our peak demand is genuinely inelastic: the customer-facing inference service has a hard latency budget, and it degrades visibly when utilization crosses about 90 percent. If our growth forecast is even roughly right, optimization buys us perhaps two quarters of runway, not a permanent reprieve. There's also a procurement reality to face: lead times on these nodes are currently eight to ten weeks. If we wait until the pain is undeniable, we will spend a painful quarter queuing behind our own decision. Ordering hardware is slow to undo but also slow to arrive; the option has a long fuse.

**Cost, risk, and reversibility**

The capital cost is real but not existential for us this year. The subtler cost is opportunity: $180k is also two engineers for a year, or the difference between hiring and not hiring on the product side. And hardware we buy is hardware we must power, cool, and eventually depreciate — a commitment that outlives the decision that created it. Optimization, by contrast, is largely reversible. If we restructure the scheduler and it turns out demand was higher than we thought, we've lost a few engineer-weeks and learned something precise about our true ceiling. If we buy nodes and demand turns out softer than forecast, we're carrying idle capital with no easy exit.

Reliability cuts both ways. More nodes means more redundancy and less exposure to a single failure taking down a class of jobs. But it also means more surface area to maintain, and our current operational load is already straining one part-time admin. Better utilization of a smaller fleet, with cleaner scheduling, is arguably the more reliable posture — provided we don't run so lean that a single node failure creates an outage rather than an inconvenience.

**Recommendation**

Do both, in sequence, with the order mattering. Start the optimization work now: scheduler improvements, reservation reform, and off-peak batch shifting. Give it six weeks and a hard success metric — peak utilization sustained below 75 percent with interactive latency within budget. Simultaneously, place a conditional purchase order for one node, not two, with delivery timed to land just after the optimization work concludes. If optimization delivers as expected, we cancel or defer the order and bank the savings. If it falls short, the hardware arrives before the situation becomes an incident.

The honest uncertainty here is demand itself. Our forecast has been wrong in both directions before, and the cheapest hedge is to keep our options open as long as possible. Sequencing a reversible intervention ahead of an irreversible purchase does exactly that. I'd like a decision by end of week so the purchase-order window doesn't slip.

Happy to walk through the utilization data with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: Hardware Purchase vs. Utilisation Improvement for Our Local Inference Capacity**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** How we should expand our AI compute capacity over the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We are approaching the practical ceiling of our current local inference hardware. Peak-hour GPU utilisation regularly exceeds 85 percent, queue times during business hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two recent incidents were caused or worsened by capacity contention rather than software faults. The instinctive response is to buy more machines. After looking at the numbers, my recommendation is that we spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of what we already own, and defer the purchase decision by roughly ninety days. If utilisation work delivers what I expect, we will still need hardware eventually, but we will need less of it, buy it later at better prices, and understand our real demand profile far more precisely when we do.

**The cost picture**

The capital case for new hardware is not as clean as it first appears. The quote we have for two additional accelerator nodes is roughly 40 percent of our annual infrastructure budget, and that figure excludes the hidden costs: rack power and cooling, which our facilities team estimates will add a recurring monthly sum; the engineering time to integrate, benchmark, and operate the new nodes; and the depreciation of equipment that historically loses resale value faster than our finance model assumes. Against that, the utilisation work is mostly labour we already pay for. Batch scheduling, model quantisation, better request coalescing, and moving batch-oriented jobs like embedding generation to overnight windows are all projects we have discussed for months and never prioritised because capacity pressure felt distant. It is no longer distant, but the cheapest capacity we can buy is the capacity we are currently wasting.

**Latency and reliability**

The counterargument, and it is a serious one, is that utilisation optimisation does not add headroom, it only moves the ceiling. Our interactive workloads are latency-sensitive, and some of our recent queueing pain is structural: we run heterogeneous models on shared nodes, and a long batch job can add hundreds of milliseconds of tail latency to a user-facing request. Better scheduling and partitioning can mitigate this, but it is genuinely uncertain whether we can recover enough effective capacity through software alone. There is also a reliability dimension. Right now, a single node failure removes a third of our serving capacity. More hardware would improve redundancy as a side effect, which is a real benefit the pure cost comparison understates. If we defer the purchase, we are accepting another quarter of elevated single-point-of-failure risk, and I think we should be honest that this is a bet.

**Opportunity cost**

Both options have opportunity costs, and they point in opposite directions. Buying hardware now consumes budget and attention that could go toward product work, and it locks us into an architecture chosen under time pressure. Improving utilisation consumes engineering hours that would otherwise go to features, and it risks becoming a distraction that delivers neither capacity nor product progress. The difference, in my view, is reversibility. Scheduling changes, quantisation, and workload placement are largely reversible and produce knowledge regardless of outcome. A hardware purchase is only partially reversible: we can resell machines, but at a loss, and the operating commitments around power and space are stickier still. When two options are close in expected value, the reversible one that teaches us more is usually the right first move.

**What would change my mind**

I want to be clear about the uncertainty here. If our utilisation audit shows that peak-hour demand is genuinely inelastic — that is, if interactive traffic alone accounts for sustained high utilisation with no batch work to displace — then software optimisation cannot save us, and we should place the hardware order immediately rather than burning a quarter pretending otherwise. I have asked for a two-week measurement exercise before we commit to the utilisation track, precisely so we are not optimising on intuition. Similarly, if the measurement shows our failure-domain risk has already materialised into customer-visible incidents, reliability may justify the purchase on its own.

**Proposed next step**

I propose we run the measurement audit over the next two weeks, then decide by a dated checkpoint whether to proceed with the utilisation quarter or trigger the purchase. Either way, we will have made the decision on evidence rather than anxiety, and that is worth the small delay.

Comments welcome before Friday.

**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal discussion draft

We've reached the point where our inference fleet is running hot most weekdays, and the question in front of us is whether to purchase additional local hardware or to invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the right answer is less obvious than the queue depths suggest, and I'd like us to decide it deliberately rather than by default.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward and emotionally compelling. Our p99 latency has crept from 400ms to nearly a second during peak hours, batch jobs are getting evicted more often, and every on-call engineer has stories about capacity contention causing an incident that shouldn't have happened. From a reliability standpoint, we're also thinner than I'd like: with our current fleet, losing a single node during peak traffic degrades service noticeably. A second node's worth of headroom would let us survive hardware failures, driver regressions, and maintenance windows without user-visible impact. Hardware is also an asset — it holds resale value reasonably well, and unlike cloud commitments, it's not a recurring bill.

But the case for better utilisation deserves a genuinely fair hearing, because our current numbers are not good. Across the fleet, our average GPU utilisation sits around 45%, and that figure flatters us; a lot of that is memory reserved by idle-but-allocated processes rather than useful compute. We have never implemented proper request batching across tenants, our model serving stack still cold-loads weights on several code paths, and our scheduling is first-come-first-served with no priority classes, which means batch work competes with latency-sensitive traffic on equal footing. Industry experience — and our own limited experiments — suggest that aggressive continuous batching plus a real scheduler could recover 30 to 50% of effective capacity. That is roughly the equivalent of one to two new nodes, at a fraction of the capital cost.

The cost comparison is where this gets interesting. A new node is roughly $90k up front plus power, cooling, and rack space, and it depreciates quickly in a market where model sizes and hardware requirements shift every eighteen months. The utilisation project, by contrast, is mostly engineering time: I estimate two engineers for six to eight weeks, with real risk of slippage. If we value that time honestly, it's not free — it's maybe $60–80k of opportunity cost, and those are engineers who would otherwise be working on product features. So the money is closer than it first appears, but the two options buy different things: hardware buys certainty, utilisation work buys capability. A better scheduler and batching layer make us permanently smarter about capacity, and that capability compounds as we grow. A node is just a node.

Reversibility matters here too. Buying hardware is a one-way door in practice — once it's racked and powered, the sunk cost anchors our architecture to it, and selling used accelerators recovers only part of the outlay. The utilisation project is almost entirely reversible: if continuous batching turns out to be a dead end for our workload mix, we've lost some weeks and learned something. That asymmetry argues for trying the cheap, reversible option before the expensive, sticky one.

There's also a timing argument. Our demand forecast is genuinely uncertain. If the new product surface launches in Q3 as hoped, we may need substantially more capacity by year end regardless of how well we optimise. If it slips or underperforms, we'll have bought hardware we don't need. Utilisation improvements are valuable in both scenarios; a new node is only clearly valuable in the first.

My recommendation, then: commit to the utilisation work now, with a hard scope and a decision checkpoint. Two engineers, eight weeks, targeting continuous batching, a priority-aware scheduler, and elimination of our worst cold-start paths. If we hit the utilisation targets and latency stays within SLO, we defer hardware purchase by at least two quarters. If we miss — either because the engineering is harder than expected or because demand grows faster than the recovered capacity — we buy the node, and we'll do so with much better information about how much headroom we actually need. I'd also propose a modest reliability hedge in the interim: a short-term cloud burst arrangement for failover capacity, which is expensive per hour but cheap as insurance and fully reversible.

My utilisation estimates come partly from vendor benchmarks that may not survive contact with our workload, and engineering estimates of this kind are routinely optimistic by 50%. **Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local GPU hardware to meet growing inference demand, or investing engineering effort to raise utilisation of the fleet we already own. By contrast, the utilisation work we propose is roughly two engineers for six to eight weeks: batch-aware request routing, a proper priority queue so interactive traffic can preempt batch jobs, and dynamic partitioning of the two large cards that are currently pinned to single tenants. The engineering cost is real, but it is an order of magnitude smaller, and unlike hardware, it compounds — every scheduling improvement we build keeps paying off as we grow.

Our p95 inference latency has degraded from 240ms to 410ms over the past quarter, and that regression is visible in user-facing metrics. Squeezing more work through existing hardware risks making this worse before it gets better; queueing discipline and batching trade throughput against tail latency, and if we get the knobs wrong, we can hurt the product while congratulating ourselves on efficiency. This is why our proposal sequences the work: we would first implement the priority queue and preemption, which should *improve* interactive latency immediately by protecting it from batch load, and only then tighten batching thresholds while watching p99 closely. If tail latency degrades beyond agreed thresholds at any point, we stop and revisit.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy — a single failed node today takes out a meaningful fraction of capacity, and a second node would halve that blast radius. But it also means more things to fail, more firmware to patch, and a larger maintenance surface for a team that is already stretched thin. Improving utilisation, by contrast, lets us consolidate workloads and take marginal nodes out of rotation, which actually improves our maintenance posture: we can drain and service machines without contention because we're no longer running everything at the edge of capacity. The reliability question is genuinely close, and we'd welcome input from SRE before finalising.

The opportunity cost deserves explicit mention. The two engineers we'd assign to utilisation work are the same people we'd want on the model-quality roadmap next quarter. Hardware purchase doesn't consume their time — but it does consume budget that could fund a third hire, and it commits us to a rack footprint and power contract that constrain next year's options. Which brings us to reversibility, the factor we weight most heavily. Hardware is nearly irreversible: cards depreciate, power contracts lock in, and if inference demand shifts to a different model size or architecture — a real possibility given how quickly our roadmap has moved this year — the fleet we buy today may be poorly matched to the workloads of eighteen months from now. Scheduling software, by contrast, is almost fully reversible and portable across whatever hardware we eventually run.

So the recommendation: fund the utilisation project now, with a checkpoint at week six. If utilisation has moved above 55% and p95 latency is back under 300ms, we defer hardware purchase entirely and re-evaluate in Q3. If the work stalls, or demand growth outpaces the gains, we execute a pre-negotiated purchase order for two nodes — sized for the *smallest* configuration that relieves contention, not the one that maximises headroom. That keeps the option open without exercising it prematurely.

We are confident in the direction and appropriately humble about the numbers. Utilisation projections are notoriously optimistic, and a single large customer onboarding could change the calculus overnight. We'll revisit this memo's assumptions monthly.

Happy to walk through the data in Thursday's infra review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference cluster

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet before committing to any new hardware purchases. The case is not that we will never need more GPUs — it is that we do not yet know enough to buy them well, and the cheapest, most reversible way to buy that knowledge is to fix what we already own.

**Where we stand**

Our eight A100s currently run at roughly 34 percent average utilisation, with a diurnal swing from under 15 percent overnight to peaks near 80 percent during business hours. That peak number is what people remember, and it is what fuels the instinct to buy. But peaks are the wrong lens. Capacity planning against peak means paying for hardware that idles most of the day, and right now we are doing exactly that with machines we already own. If we cannot get our current fleet above 60 percent sustained, buying more of the same will not solve the underlying problem; it will simply double the amount of idle capacity we are amortising.

**Cost**

The purchase option is expensive in more ways than the invoice. A two-node expansion would cost approximately $380K upfront, plus roughly $4K monthly in power, cooling, and colocation. More importantly, it is a bet on our current workload shape staying constant. GPU generations turn over every 18 to 24 months, and hardware bought today at peak pricing will be worth a fraction of that on the secondary market when our needs change. Depreciation on underused accelerators is the quietest and largest waste in most ML budgets, and we would be adding to it.

By contrast, the utilisation work — batch scheduling, request coalescing, quantisation of our two largest models, and a proper queueing layer — is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway. Even attributing two engineers for a quarter, the cost is a fraction of the hardware option, and it produces assets (scheduling infrastructure, telemetry) that retain value regardless of what we eventually buy.

**Latency**

The honest counterargument is latency. Our interactive workloads have a p95 budget of 400ms, and coalescing requests or batching more aggressively trades tail latency for throughput. This is a real risk, but it is a managed one: modern continuous batching can raise throughput substantially while keeping tail latency within budget, and we can enforce per-tenant SLOs at the queue layer. If utilisation work pushes p95 past acceptable bounds, we will know quickly and can dial back — a feedback loop measured in days, not procurement cycles.

**Reliability**

There is also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy against node failure, and our current single-node failure does degrade service for the affected model. But redundancy bought through utilisation improvements — better failover, faster checkpoint recovery, workload migration — addresses the same risk more cheaply. And a larger fleet with poor scheduling is arguably less reliable in practice, because capacity is harder to reason about when it is spread thin across more machines with low headroom everywhere.

**Opportunity cost**

The deeper question is what else the money could do. $380K is roughly a year of a senior engineer, or the entire budget for our evaluation and safety tooling, which is currently underfunded. Buying hardware that sits idle 60 percent of the time is a decision to fund silicon instead of people, and given that our bottleneck over the next two quarters is more likely to be model quality and evaluation than raw throughput, that trade looks wrong to me.

**Reversibility**

Finally, reversibility. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible at our scale — resale value is poor, and the commitment shapes our architecture for years. Utilisation work is the opposite: every piece of it (scheduling, batching, quantisation) is additive and reversible, and it makes a future purchase *more* effective, because whatever we buy later will arrive into a fleet that knows how to use it. Buying hardware now, before the utilisation work, would mean paying full price to defer a problem we could have solved cheaply.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear about what we do not know. Our traffic forecast has wide error bars; if the new customer pipeline closes, demand could double within two quarters, and utilisation work alone would not cover that. There is also lead-time risk: if we decide in Q3 that we do need hardware, a 10–14 week procurement delay could hurt. To hedge, I propose we begin vendor qualification now — pricing, lead times, and a small evaluation unit if one is available — so that a purchase decision in Q3 is fast rather than cold-started. That keeps the option open at near-zero cost.

**Decision requested**

Approve one

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide whether to purchase additional local GPU hardware or to invest in improving utilisation of the fleet we already own. After several weeks of measurement, modelling, and argument, we have a recommendation, though it comes with honest caveats about what we still don't know.

**The current situation**

Our four A100-class nodes are, on paper, capable of handling our current workload mix — inference for the internal assistant, batch embedding jobs, and the training runs our research group schedules a few times a month. In practice, average utilisation sits around 38 percent, but that number is misleading. Peak demand on weekday afternoons pushes two of the four nodes to saturation, and the research team's training jobs, which can't be preempted without losing days of work, block inference capacity for hours at a time. The result is that our p95 inference latency has crept from 400ms to over 2 seconds during peak windows, which is now visibly degrading the assistant experience and generating complaints from the support team.

The obvious fix is to buy two more nodes. At current pricing that's roughly $180k in capital plus perhaps $15k annually in power, cooling, and maintenance. That's not a catastrophic sum for us, but it's not trivial either, and it would consume most of our remaining hardware budget for the year.

**Why we don't think buying is the right first move**

The strongest argument against purchasing is that we would be buying capacity to serve a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. Our analysis suggests that if we implemented proper workload partitioning — reserving two nodes for latency-sensitive inference, one for batch, and one as a flexible pool — we could hold p95 latency under 700ms at current demand without any new hardware. The training jobs would run overnight or on the flexible node with queueing, which the research team has informally agreed to tolerate if it means the assistant stops timing out.

There's also the opportunity cost to weigh. That $180k spent on GPUs is $180k not spent on the observability overhaul we've deferred twice, or on the storage expansion that our dataset team has been requesting since spring. Hardware depreciates quickly in this market; the A100s we'd buy today will be worth a fraction of that in three years, and the rental market for on-demand capacity has never been cheaper if we hit a genuine crunch.

Reversibility matters too. Buying hardware is a one-way door in practical terms — once purchased, the money is gone, and the sunk-cost pressure to keep the machines busy will distort future decisions. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible. If our scheduling changes prove too disruptive, we can revert in an afternoon. If they succeed, we'll have bought ourselves time and, more importantly, information: a much better picture of our true demand curve before we commit capital against it.

**What we propose**

We recommend a three-month programme of utilisation work: workload partitioning, a proper job queue with priorities, autoscaling of batch work into off-peak windows, and better per-tenant metering so we can see who is actually consuming what. The engineering cost is roughly six weeks of one engineer's time, which is real but modest. We'd set explicit success criteria: p95 inference latency under 700ms sustained, training job turnaround under 24 hours, and utilisation above 55 percent. If we hit those targets and demand keeps growing, the case for a purchase in the next budget cycle becomes strong and well-evidenced rather than reactive.

**Honest uncertainty**

We should be candid about the risks. Our demand forecast is based on twelve months of history, and if the assistant's usage doubles after the planned product launch, utilisation work alone won't save us — we'd be buying hardware under time pressure, which is when organisations make their worst procurement decisions. There's also a real chance the scheduling work is harder than we estimate; preemption and partitioning on shared GPU infrastructure has burned better teams than ours. And the research group's patience with queueing is an assumption, not a commitment.

On balance, though, the asymmetry favours waiting. The cost of six weeks of engineering time is small; the cost of $180k spent on hardware we may not need, or of buying in a panic later, is large. We recommend proceeding with the utilisation programme immediately and revisiting the purchase decision with real data in Q3.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data in detail at Thursday's review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next six to eight weeks improving utilisation of our existing GPU fleet before committing to any new hardware purchases. If utilisation improvements stall below roughly 55 percent sustained, or if product demand accelerates faster than our current forecast, we should revisit the purchase decision with better data in hand. This is not a deferral for its own sake; it is the cheapest way to buy information, and the option value of waiting is currently higher than the cost of occasional queuing.

**The situation**

Our four A100 nodes currently run at an average of 38 percent utilisation, but that average hides a problematic pattern. Utilisation peaks above 85 percent during business hours in our primary region and drops below 15 percent overnight and on weekends. Meanwhile, our latency SLO is breached roughly twice a week during peak windows, and the obvious fix — buying two more nodes — has been proposed. The capital cost is significant: approximately $180K upfront, plus roughly $2K per month per node in power, cooling, and colocation, and a realistic three-year depreciation horizon given how quickly inference-optimised hardware is improving.

**Why buying now is the wrong first move**

The case for buying rests on a real problem, but it treats our worst hour as if it were our average hour. We are not capacity-constrained in any meaningful sense for most of the week; we are peak-constrained for a few hours a day. Buying hardware to solve a peak problem means paying for idle metal the rest of the time. Before we spend $180K on capacity that sits dormant 70 percent of the hours in a week, we should exhaust the much cheaper levers.

Those levers are well understood. Batch size tuning alone has historically yielded 20 to 30 percent throughput gains in systems like ours, at the cost of a modest latency increase that our SLOs can absorb. Better request routing, quantisation of our two largest models, aggressive caching of common completions, and time-shifting our internal batch evaluation jobs to off-peak windows would together plausibly lift effective capacity by 40 to 60 percent. None of this is speculative engineering; it is mostly configuration, measurement, and discipline. The engineering cost is perhaps three to four engineer-weeks — a rounding error against the capital purchase.

**Latency and reliability considerations**

I want to be honest about the trade-off here. Some utilisation improvements, particularly larger batch sizes, trade throughput for tail latency. Our p99 currently sits at 1.9 seconds; pushing batches harder could push it toward 2.4 seconds unless we implement admission control. That is why the work must include a proper load-shedding and priority-queueing layer, not just tuning knobs. Reliability is the other argument people reach for when advocating more hardware: more nodes means more redundancy. That is true, but our recent incidents were caused by a misconfigured load balancer and a stuck batch job, not by capacity exhaustion. Redundancy purchased to mask operational fragility tends to hide problems rather than fix them. The reliability work — better canaries, circuit breakers, and automated failover drills — is needed regardless and is independent of fleet size.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The $180K we would spend on hardware is money not spent on hiring, on evaluation infrastructure, or simply preserved as runway. Hardware purchases are also poorly reversible: GPUs depreciate fast, resale is messy, and colocation contracts lock us in. Utilisation work, by contrast, is almost perfectly reversible — if a batching change hurts latency, we roll it back in an afternoon. When one option is reversible and the other is not, and both address the same symptom, we should exhaust the reversible one first. This is a decision under uncertainty, and the asymmetry favours waiting.

**What would change my mind**

If our demand forecast shows sustained growth that utilisation gains cannot absorb, or if a strategic commitment (a large customer, a latency-sensitive product launch) makes tail-latency risk unacceptable, we should buy — and we should buy with headroom rather than at the margin, because incremental GPU purchases are operationally more expensive than step changes. I have asked Priya to draft a utilisation-improvement plan with weekly checkpoints; we will present measured results in six weeks.

**Decision requested:** Endorse the utilisation-first approach and the six-week checkpoint before any capital approval.
